name: 1st Sunday in Lent
description: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness. The struggle against evil.
biblicalBasis: After his baptism, Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness where he fasts for 40 days and is tempted by the devil (Matt 4:1-11, Luke 4:1-13). Three temptations: to turn stones into bread (self-gratification), to throw himself down from the temple (to test God), and to worship the devil in exchange for the kingdoms of the world (power). Jesus rejects all with Scripture quotes from Deuteronomy.
significance: Jesus undergoes the trial that Israel failed — 40 years in the wilderness with grumbling and idolatry. Where Israel fell, Jesus stands firm. The temptations represent fundamental human temptations: satisfaction of needs, prestige, and power. Jesus' answers show that God's word is the weapon against temptation.
liturgicalContext: Purple color. First Sunday in Lent. The account of the temptation is read every year — it sets the tone for the entire Lenten season as a time of struggle.
history: The account of the temptation has been linked to the 1st Sunday in Lent since the early church. The 40 days in the wilderness provided the model for Lent. Many Church Fathers saw the temptations as a summary of all human temptations.
otConnections: Israel's 40 years in the wilderness (Deut 8:2-3) — Jesus quotes directly from Deuteronomy. Adam's temptation in the garden (Gen 3) — the new Adam stands firm where the first fell. Moses' 40 days on Sinai (Exod 34:28). Elijah's 40 days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8).

references.reason: The day is defined by the account of Jesus' temptation in the wilderness. Matt 4:1-11 is the main text describing the 40 days of fasting and the three temptations, which are central to Lenten theology regarding the struggle against evil and Jesus' victory where Israel failed.

Jesus' answer as to why his disciples do not fast: 'Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?' (v. 15). This is a direct theological link to the 1st Sunday in Lent, which focuses on the meaning of fasting and the transition from the presence of the bridegroom to mourning and fasting when he is taken away.

The 1st Sunday in Lent concerns Jesus' temptation and the struggle against evil. Matthew 18:1-14 with its call to repentance ('turn back') and warning to remove what causes stumbling (hand, foot, eye) is a very strong parallel to the theme at the start of Lent about cleaning up one's own life and fighting sin.
